q.t: In the 2009 Citizenship Survey, what percentage of people identified themselves as Christian?
q.e: The UK is historically a Christian country. In the 2009 Citizenship Survey, 70% of people identified themselves as Christian. In the Citizenship Survey, 21% of people said that they had no religion.

q.t: In the Citizenship Survey, what percentage of people said that they had no religion?
q.e: Much smaller proportions identified themselves as Muslim (4%), Hindu (2%), Sikh (1%), Jewish or Buddhist (both less than 0.5%), and 2% of people followed another religion. In the Citizenship Survey, 21% of people said that they had no religion.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Much smaller proportions identified themselves as Muslim (4%), Hindu (2%), Sikh (1%), Jewish or Buddhist (both less than 0.5%).
o: A larger proportion identified themselves as Muslim than as Hindu
A larger proportion identified themselves as Hindu than as Muslim

q.t: Which TWO places of worship are named in the handbook for religions other than Christianity?
q.e: There are religious buildings for other religions all over the UK. This includes Islamic mosques, Hindu temples, Jewish synagogues, Sikh gurdwaras and Buddhist temples.

q.t: Since when has the Church of England existed?
q.e: The official Church of the state is the Church of England. It is a Protestant Church and has existed since the Reformation in the 1530s.

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Several Church of England bishops sit in the House of Lords.
q.e: The monarch is the head of the Church of England. The spiritual leader of the Church of England is the Archbishop of Canterbury. Several Church of England bishops sit in the House of Lords.

q.t: What was the population of the UK in 1901, according to the handbook's table?
q.e: The table of population growth in the UK shows: 1801, 8 million; 1851, 20 million; 1901, 40 million; 1951, 50 million; 1998, 57 million.

q.t: According to the handbook's table, what was the population of the UK in 1851?
q.e: The table of population growth in the UK shows: 1600, just over 4 million; 1700, 5 million; 1801, 8 million; 1851, 20 million; 1901, 40 million.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: The population is very unequally distributed over the four parts of the UK. England more or less consistently makes up 84% of the total population, Wales around 5%, Scotland just over 8% and Northern Ireland less than 3%.
o: Wales has a larger share of the UK population than Northern Ireland
Northern Ireland has a larger share of the UK population than Wales

q.t: Why are people in the UK living longer than ever before?
q.e: People in the UK are living longer than ever before. This is due to improved living standards and better health care. There are now a record number of people aged 85 and over. This has an impact on the cost of pensions and health care.
o: Improved living standards and better health care
A fall in the birth rate

q.t: In surveys, which is the most common ethnic description chosen?
q.e: In surveys, the most common ethnic description chosen is white, which includes people of European, Australian, Canadian, New Zealand and American descent. Other significant groups are those of Asian, black and mixed descent.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: Women in Britain today make up about half of the workforce. On average, girls leave school with better qualifications than boys. More women than men study at university.
o: More women than men study at university
More men than women study at university

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
In the UK it is a legal requirement that men and women should not be discriminated against because of their gender or because they are, or are not, married.
q.e: Within the UK, it is a legal requirement that men and women should not be discriminated against because of their gender or because they are, or are not, married. They have equal rights to work, own property, marry and divorce.

q.t: Which day comes immediately before Lent begins?
q.e: The day before Lent starts is called Shrove Tuesday, or Pancake Day. People eat pancakes, which were traditionally made to use up foods such as eggs, fat and milk before fasting. Lent begins on Ash Wednesday.

q.t: How many days before Easter does Lent last?
q.e: The 40 days before Easter are known as Lent. It is a time when Christians take time to reflect and prepare for Easter. Traditionally, people would fast during this period and today many people will give something up.

q.t: Which TWO days at Easter are public holidays?
q.e: Easter takes place in March or April. It marks the death of Jesus Christ on Good Friday and his rising from the dead on Easter Sunday. Both Good Friday and the following Monday, called Easter Monday, are public holidays.

q.t: When is Mothering Sunday?
q.e: Mothering Sunday, or Mother's Day, is the Sunday three weeks before Easter. Children send cards or buy gifts for their mothers. Father's Day is the third Sunday in June.
o: The Sunday three weeks before Easter

q.t: How long does Hannukah last, and what does it remember?
q.e: Hannukah is in November or December and is celebrated for eight days. It is to remember the Jews' struggle for religious freedom. On each day of the festival a candle is lit on a stand of eight candles, called a menorah.
o: Eight days, remembering the Jews' struggle for religious freedom
Five days, remembering the Jews' struggle for religious freedom
Eight days, remembering the founding of the Khalsa
Eight days, remembering the end of Ramadan

q.t: On which date is Vaisakhi celebrated?
q.e: Vaisakhi, also spelled Baisakhi, is a Sikh festival which celebrates the founding of the Sikh community known as the Khalsa. It is celebrated on 14 April each year with parades, dancing and singing.

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: In Scotland, 31 December is called Hogmanay and 2 January is also a public holiday. For some Scottish people, Hogmanay is a bigger holiday than Christmas.
o: In Scotland, 2 January is also a public holiday
In Scotland, 2 January is an ordinary working day

q.t: Until what time of day do people play jokes on April Fool's Day?
q.e: April Fool's Day, 1 April, is a day when people play jokes on each other until midday. The television and newspapers often have stories that are April Fool jokes.

q.t: What happened in 1605 that Bonfire Night commemorates?
q.e: Bonfire Night, 5 November, is an occasion when people in Great Britain set off fireworks. The origin of this celebration was an event in 1605, when a group of Catholics led by Guy Fawkes failed in their plan to kill the Protestant king with a bomb in the Houses of Parliament.
o: A group of Catholics led by Guy Fawkes failed in a plan to kill the Protestant king
A group of Protestants failed in a plan to kill the Catholic king
The Houses of Parliament burned down
The Gunpowder was discovered at the Tower of London

q.t: Where are wreaths laid on Remembrance Day?
q.e: Remembrance Day, 11 November, commemorates those who died fighting for the UK and its allies. People wear poppies. At 11.00 am there is a two-minute silence and wreaths are laid at the Cenotaph in Whitehall, London.
o: At the Cenotaph in Whitehall, London

q.t: Which additional public holiday is marked in Northern Ireland in July?
q.e: There are other public holidays each year called bank holidays. These are of no religious significance. They are at the beginning of May, in late May or early June, and in August. In Northern Ireland, the anniversary of the Battle of the Boyne in July is also a public holiday.
o: The anniversary of the Battle of the Boyne
The anniversary of the Easter Rising
